concepts.name: Estimating vector storage for a large corpus
pgvector index limits and filtered search
Ingestion at scale and incremental updates
Hybrid search and the cost of reranking

questions.prompt: You index 1,000,000 PDFs at 50 chunks each, with 1,536-dimension embeddings stored in a pgvector `vector` column. pgvector stores each vector in `4 * dimensions + 8` bytes. About how much space do the vectors alone take?

choices.text: About 31 GB
About 77 GB
About 3 TB
About 308 GB

questions.explanation: Chunks: 1,000,000 × 50 = 50,000,000. Bytes per vector: 4 × 1,536 + 8 = 6,152. Total: 50,000,000 × 6,152 ≈ 307.6 billion bytes, about 308 GB. That's before the HNSW index, the chunk text and metadata, which add a lot more. Option b is what you'd get with 1 byte per dimension; a and c are off by 10×.

questions.prompt: You switch to a 3,072-dimension embedding model and run `CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)` on a `vector(3072)` column. What happens?

choices.text: It works, but each query is about twice as slow as with a 1,536-dimension model
It fails: HNSW indexes `vector` only up to 2,000 dimensions; use `halfvec` (up to 4,000) or fewer dimensions
It fails, because pgvector can't store any `vector` value longer than 2,000 dimensions, whether indexed or not
It succeeds, but silently truncates each vector to its first 2,000 dimensions before indexing

questions.explanation: pgvector can store `vector` values up to 16,000 dimensions, but its HNSW and IVFFlat indexes support `vector` only up to 2,000. `halfvec` (half-precision) can be indexed up to 4,000 dimensions and takes `2 * dimensions + 8` bytes, half the space. Another fix is an embedding model or setting with fewer dimensions.

questions.prompt: This Lesson's exercise: estimate storage for a million PDFs. Explain the formula, what else takes space beyond the raw vectors, and how you would shrink it.

model_answer.summary: Storage is roughly documents × chunks per document × bytes per vector, plus the index, the chunk text and metadata; halving precision, cutting dimensions or quantising shrinks it.
key_points: Number of vectors = PDFs × chunks per PDF (for example 1M × 50 = 50M)
Bytes per vector in pgvector's `vector` type are `4 * dimensions + 8`, so 1,536 dimensions take about 6 KB and 50M vectors about 308 GB
The ANN index (such as HNSW), the chunk text and metadata columns add substantially to the raw vector size
`halfvec` halves vector storage, and a lower-dimension embedding shrinks it in proportion
Binary quantisation stores a compact bit vector for a fast first pass, with re-ranking on full vectors

questions.explanation: The interview wants the formula stated before the number, and the awareness that the index and text are part of the bill. pgvector's README gives the per-vector sizes, the `halfvec` option and binary quantisation.

questions.prompt: Each night about 2% of the million PDFs change and a few are deleted. What is the best way to keep the index current?

choices.text: Rebuild the whole index from scratch every night, so it can never drift from the source files
Append new chunks for changed PDFs and leave old ones in place, so earlier versions stay searchable
Compare content hashes; replace changed PDFs' chunks in one transaction, delete removed PDFs' chunks
Re-embed every PDF whose file modification time changed, which is cheaper than hashing the content

questions.explanation: Comparing a content hash finds exactly the PDFs that changed, so you only re-extract and re-embed about 2% of the corpus. Replacing a document's chunks in one transaction avoids a window where old and new versions both appear. Appending leaves stale chunks that retrieval will still return, and a full rebuild wastes 98% of the work. Modification times change without content changes, so they cause needless re-embedding.

questions.prompt: What architecture suits the initial ingestion of a million PDFs?

choices.text: A document queue, workers running idempotent per-document jobs, retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue
One script that loops over all PDFs in order and stops at the first failure so nothing is skipped
Processing each PDF inside its upload HTTP request, so users see searchable results straight away
One large transaction that inserts every chunk, so any failure rolls everything back cleanly

questions.explanation: At this scale, some PDFs will be corrupt and some API calls will fail. A queue lets you scale workers, retry transient failures with backoff, and park documents that keep failing in a dead-letter queue for inspection. Idempotent jobs (keyed by document ID and content hash) make retries safe. Batch embedding calls to cut per-request overhead.

questions.prompt: Describe how you'd keep a million-PDF index up to date as documents are added, edited and deleted.

model_answer.summary: Track each document's identity and content hash, process only what changed through a queue, replace a document's chunks atomically, and remove chunks of deleted documents.
key_points: Each document has a stable ID and a stored content hash; a change is detected by comparing hashes
New and changed documents go on a queue for extraction, chunking and embedding by workers
A changed document's old chunks are deleted and new ones inserted in one transaction, so retrieval never mixes versions
Deleted source documents have their chunks deleted too, so retrieval doesn't return content that no longer exists
Changing the embedding model or chunking means re-embedding everything, ideally into a new index you switch to when it's complete

questions.explanation: Incremental updates are a correctness problem as much as a cost one: stale or duplicate chunks lead to wrong answers with citations to outdated text. The last point matters because vectors from different embedding models can't be mixed in one index.

questions.prompt: Why combine keyword search (such as BM25 or Postgres full-text search) with embedding search over the PDFs?

choices.text: Hybrid search is cheaper than running either kind of search on its own
Embeddings can't represent chunks longer than a sentence, so keywords fill the gap
pgvector requires a full-text index before it can build a vector index
Keywords catch exact terms such as part numbers and names; embeddings catch synonyms and paraphrases

questions.explanation: Applied-llms.org puts it this way: a hybrid works best, keyword matching for the obvious matches and embeddings for synonyms, hypernyms and spelling errors. Exact identifiers like `INV-2024-0042` are where pure embedding search often fails. pgvector's docs show combining it with Postgres full-text search and merging results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

questions.prompt: You retrieve the top 150 chunks per query and rerank them with a cross-encoder to pick the top 20. What does the reranking cost scale with?

choices.text: The number of candidates per query times the number of queries, not the corpus size
The total number of chunks in the index, so it grows as you add PDFs
Nothing per query: it's a one-time cost paid when documents are indexed
Only the dimensions of the embedding model

questions.explanation: A reranker scores each (query, candidate) pair at query time, so its cost and latency grow with candidates per query × queries. Cutting candidates from 150 to 50 cuts that work about 3×, at some risk to recall. Anthropic's contextual retrieval post uses top-150 then top-20 and notes that reranking adds latency at runtime.

questions.prompt: Users may only see PDFs their team has access to. Where should that rule be enforced?

choices.text: In the system prompt: tell the model not to quote documents the user can't access
By checking the final answer and hiding it if it mentions a restricted document
In the retrieval query, filtering by the user's permissions so restricted chunks never reach the prompt
By training a separate embedding model for each team

questions.explanation: Once a restricted chunk is in the prompt, no instruction reliably stops the model from using it, and prompt injection can undo such instructions. OWASP's LLM08 (vector and embedding weaknesses) recommends permission-aware vector stores and strict partitioning so one group's data can't be retrieved for another. Filter by ACL metadata (or partition per tenant) inside the query.

questions.prompt: With an HNSW index and the default `hnsw.ef_search` of 40, you run `... WHERE team_id = 7 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10`. Team 7 owns 10% of the rows. The query often returns only about 4 rows. Why, and what helps?

choices.text: `LIMIT` is ignored by HNSW index scans, so rows get dropped; add `OFFSET 0` to force the planner to apply it
The filter applies after the scan, so ~10% of 40 candidates match; use iterative scans or a partial index
HNSW returns at most 4 rows per graph layer visited; switch to IVFFlat, which has no such cap
The planner caches results from earlier queries; run `VACUUM` before each query to refresh them

questions.explanation: With approximate indexes pgvector applies the `WHERE` filter after the index scan. With `ef_search` 40 and a filter matching 10% of rows, about 4 rows survive on average, which is the README's own example. Fixes: iterative index scans (pgvector 0.8.0+, `hnsw.iterative_scan`), a higher `ef_search`, a partial index per team, or partitioning. This matters for access-control filters.

questions.prompt: Explain how you'd implement access control for question answering over a million PDFs shared by many teams, and why instructions in the prompt aren't enough.

model_answer.summary: Store each chunk's permissions with it and filter on the user's permissions inside retrieval (or partition data per tenant), so the model only ever sees text the user may read.
key_points: Each chunk carries ACL metadata copied from its source document, such as team or tenant IDs
Retrieval filters on the requesting user's permissions in the same query, or searches only that tenant's partition
Permission changes on a source document must update its chunks' metadata promptly
Prompt instructions aren't a control: once text is in the context the model can reveal it, and injected text can override instructions
Test it: queries from one team must never retrieve another team's chunks, including with filters that make ANN search return few results

questions.explanation: OWASP lists unauthorised access and cross-tenant leaks from shared vector stores as a top LLM risk and recommends permission-aware stores with logical partitioning. The last point ties to pgvector's filtering behaviour: a filter applied after an approximate index scan changes how many results you get, so test it.
